newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL CAPITAL GOODS SALES SEEN SLOWING TRADE GAP.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL CAPITAL GOODS SALES SEEN SLOWING TRADE GAP.

text.p: An upturn in sales of Brazilian capital goods might slow Brazil's widening trade gap in 1997, the private National Industry Confederation (CNI) said Thursday.

The CNI now expects Brazil to post a trade deficit of between $10 and $11 billion for the year as a whole, down from a previous prediction of $15 billion, CNI president Fernando Bezerra told reporters.
Brazil posted a trade deficit of $5.52 billion in the first seven months of the year, virtually the same as the total shortfall in 1996.
"Brazilian industry is completing a cycle of modernization, and the numbers point to growth in exports," Bezerra said.
CNI data showed sales of capital goods were recovering after slumping earlier in the year.

After a 8.08 percent fall in the first quarter when compared with the same period in 1996, capital goods sales were down just 0.6 percent in the second quarter and in the month of June rose 6.7 percent versus the same month last year.
Sales of electro-domestic goods, which were on the increase in the first quarter of the year, appeared to be heading in the opposite direction, falling 12.2 percent in June.
"Electro-domestic goods are leaving the scene to be replaced by capital goods," said Jose Guilherme dos Reis, head of the CNI's economics department.

The slump in consumer goods sales reflected slower growth in the average spending power of Brazilian workers which in the first half of 1997 rose one percent, compared to a seven percent increase in the same period last year, dos Reis said.
However, while the growth in capital goods sales was good news for exports, the recent devaluation of several Asian currencies might expose Brazil to cheaper imports from those countries, he warned.
The outlook for industry sales as a whole for the second half of 1997 was positive although the 10 percent growth seen between January and June was unlikely to be matched, dos Reis said.
Car sales, which rose 26.7 percent in the first half of the year and 32.5 percent in the second quarter, were key to industrial performance in the rest of the 1997, he said.
